Home and pension wealth: compare similar families, then check the cash

Compare official homeownership and employer-pension wealth medians for younger and pre-retirement families, then build a separate cash stress with two editable graphics.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Read the survey, then test a separate cash position

Interactive planning lab

Hypothetical net worth$970,000
Cash needed for the separate six-month stress$32,000
Additional cash needed in that stress$12,000

The first two charts are fixed official 2023 survey observations, released 29 October 2024 and reviewed 25 October 2026. Controls change only the last two hypothetical charts. Net home equity is already after the mortgage. Other inputs are non-overlapping net asset amounts. The cash stress assumes six months without income, zero interest, a bill at time zero and monthly essentials, without selling assets, drawing pensions or borrowing. It is not a percentile calculator or a recommended reserve size.

On this page

  1. Read the population, date and unit first

The central idea

A wealth median describes a particular group at a particular date. It does not tell you how much cash a family can spend or what your own plan needs.

01

Read the population, date and unit first

Statistics Canada’s 2023 Survey of Financial Security release, published on 29 October 2024, reports family wealth in 2023 constant Canadian dollars. “Families” includes economic families and unattached individuals. Age refers to the major income earner. Coverage is the ten provinces, excluding Indigenous communities and collective dwellings.

These observations describe 2023, even when you read the article in 2026. They are not current account balances. The sample has sampling variability and does not adequately represent the very wealthy; the release supplies no confidence intervals for the selected comparisons.

The age and provincial wealth guide provides broader context. Here the focus is how housing and pension status change comparisons within selected age groups.

Before using any benchmark, write down four items: who was measured, when they were measured, which balance-sheet definition was used, and whether the statistic is a median or mean. A number with the wrong denominator can be precise and still answer the wrong question.

02

Keep housing and pension status visible

Among families with a major income earner under 35, median net worth was CAD 457,100 with a principal residence and CAD 44,000 without one. For ages 55–64, the four displayed medians range from CAD 11,900 with neither a principal home nor an employer pension to a rounded CAD 1.4 million with both.

The bars show group differences. They do not measure what would happen if the same family bought a home tomorrow, nor isolate housing from earnings, age within the band, borrowing or other circumstances. Treat them as context for a question, rather than the answer to a purchase decision.

A median is the middle observation after ordering the measured values. It is neither an average account balance nor a recommended target. A family above a median may have an unaffordable monthly budget; another below it may have reliable income and modest future spending needs.

03

Build your own balance sheet without double counting

The independent worked example has CAD 600,000 of net home equity, CAD 250,000 of pension and restricted assets, CAD 100,000 of other investments and CAD 20,000 of uncommitted cash. These non-overlapping amounts add to CAD 970,000.

The example is not a reconstruction of a median family. It deliberately combines a large balance-sheet total with a much smaller immediate cash amount so the two planning jobs remain visible.

Net home equity is already after the mortgage. Entering equity and then deducting the same mortgage again would understate net worth. Conversely, entering the home’s gross value as equity would overstate it. A fuller balance sheet would list each asset and liability separately, with a valuation date and consistent ownership share.

Use care with pension values. A benefit valuation may belong on a balance sheet without being a bank account you can withdraw. If pension income already funds retirement spending in another projection, do not also spend its entire balance-sheet value as available cash in that same projection.

04

Give immediately available cash its own test

The last graphic assumes income stops for six months. Essential bills are CAD 4,000 per month and an additional CAD 8,000 bill arrives immediately. Required cash is therefore 8,000 + 6 × 4,000 = CAD 32,000.

Against CAD 20,000 of uncommitted cash, the unfunded need is CAD 12,000. The CAD 970,000 net-worth total does not settle that difference automatically. This model does not sell investments, borrow against a property or draw pension benefits.

That is a deliberately narrow stress, not a recommendation that every family hold six months of the same expenses. Actual needs depend on job income, available support, payment dates, insurance and the consequences of selling assets. FCAC’s goal-setting guidance identifies access to short-term savings as a separate consideration.

05

Change one component and ask what actually improved

Increase home equity by CAD 100,000 while leaving cash unchanged. The hypothetical net-worth waterfall increases by CAD 100,000, but the six-month funding gap stays CAD 12,000. That is the distinction between balance-sheet value and resources assigned to a payment.

Next increase cash by CAD 12,000 while keeping all other fields unchanged. The stress becomes fully funded and net worth also rises. This edit assumes new resources: it does not represent moving money from investments to cash. To model a transfer, reduce investments by the same amount so total wealth remains constant.

For a practical review, keep three separate records: a dated balance sheet, a calendar of spending and receipts, and a list of assets that could become cash with their costs and restrictions. Review progress against your own obligations and goals alongside any population comparison.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. The first two graphics reproduce selected 2023 Survey of Financial Security observations. The balance-sheet and cash-stress graphics are independent hypothetical examples, and changing their controls never changes the official observations. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope. Recheck current issuer documents for any product-specific decision.

  1. Statistics Canada · Survey of Financial Security, 2023 ↗

    Released 29 October 2024; live official HTML retrieved and checked 25 October 2026. Supports the six selected medians, family/age definitions, 2023 constant-dollar units, survey exclusions and sampling limitations. The CAD 1.4 million observation retains the release’s rounding. No medians are added together and no percentile, causal effect or 2026 valuation is inferred.

  2. FCAC · Setting savings and investment goals ↗

    Reviewed 25 October 2026 for identifying amounts, deadlines, changing priorities and the need for accessible short-term savings. The scenario amounts and rules are independently authored; this source does not endorse the calculators.
